articles.title: Trump delivers speech to rows of empty seats ‘deep in heart of Trump country’: report
articles.description: President Donald Trump delivered his rally speech in Tennessee Saturday to entire sections of empty seats at the F&M Bank Arena in Clarksville, new video and photos of the rally revealed. “President Trump’s crowd on a Saturday afternoon in Clarksville, Tennessee, near the Kentucky border, deep in the heart of Trump country,” wrote New York Times reporter Shawn McCreesh in a social media post on X, alongside a video showing entire seating sections devoid of attendees. Reuters photographer Seth Herald also captured a photo featuring “a section of empty seats” at the arena while Trump delivered his rally speech, which was disrupted within minutes by a heckler. Trump’s rally in Clarksville comes just weeks ahead of the midterms. Republicans have injected an “unprecedented flood of late ad spending” in “longtime Republican states and districts,” with Republicans increasingly distancing themselves from the president as his approval ratings continue to plummet to career lows amid his deeply unpopular war against Iran. Near the beginning of the rally, Trump complained about what he argued was inadequate press coverage of his rally sizes, an increasingly frequent grievance. An analysis by The Daily Beast’s investigative unit PunchUp found that Trump’s latest rallies have been held in venues much smaller than those he filled during his first presidential campaign, and with crowds as much as 75% smaller. Trump lashed out Monday at reports of thin crowds, insisting on Truth Social that one of his recent arenas was “totally MAXED OUT, including all upper sections.” The New York Times had reported “swaths of empty seats” at his rally in Mobile, Alabama, where he drew about 8,000 people to a 10,000-seat basketball arena. In 2015, he packed more than 30,000 into a football stadium in the same city.

articles.title: The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton Ash
articles.description: Moscow’s imperialist strongman believes decadent European democracies can be cowed. Our job is to prove him wrong Vladimir Putin is escalating both his full-scale war against Ukraine and his shadow war against the rest of Europe. His main purpose in the shadow one is to break European support for Ukraine so he can subjugate that country, something he regards as existential for Russia’s future and his own. While we in the rest of Europe must prepare as best we can to defend ourselves against every kind of hybrid attack, the central thrust of our response should be to redouble our support for Ukraine. Ukraine is his main target. It’s there, and only there, not in a contest of a thousand hybrid pinpricks, that Putin’s Russia can in a meaningful sense be defeated and deterred. In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology. He reminds us that in 2016 Putin said “Russia’s frontier ends nowhere” and in 2025, “wherever the boot of a Russian soldier steps, that is ours”. West Europeans, fondly imagining that we have consigned such brute territorial imperialism to the dustbin of history, tend to think there must be some other explanation (eg something we did “wrong”, like the eastward expansion of Nato). Finns, Estonians and Poles know better. Despite Russia’s weaknesses, the author concludes, it is “the most dangerous country in the world”. Some in Asia might question that large claim, but certainly Russia is the most dangerous country for Europe. Continue reading...
